paper_a.title: A Simple Proof of the Johnson--Lindenstrauss Extension Theorem

paper_b.title: On Sparsity and Sub-Gaussianity in the Johnson-Lindenstrauss Lemma

metadata.description: Both papers revolve around Johnson-Lindenstrauss-type machinery. Paper A proves the JL EXTENSION theorem (any Lipschitz map from an n-point subset into Hilbert space extends to the superspace with a sqrt(log n) Lipschitz blow-up) via Gaussian-coordinate isometry + McShane extension + a maximum-of-squared-Gaussians bound. Paper B extends the underlying JL LEMMA (dimensionality reduction) to sub-Gaussian and sparse projection matrices with an explicit sparsity threshold and an Achlioptas-optimality result. They share the central concentration ingredient (squared (sub-)Gaussian tail bounds yielding the log n factor), but treat different downstream problems (Lipschitz extension vs. dimension reduction).

matches.explanation: Paper A's main result is the JL EXTENSION theorem (Lipschitz extension with sqrt(log n) blow-up); paper B's main classical result is the standard JL LEMMA (dimension reduction with d >= 8 log n / (eps^2 - eps^3)). Both are 'JL-type' theorems and both rely on the same log n concentration phenomenon, but they answer different existence questions: extension of a Lipschitz map vs. existence of a low-dimensional embedding. Aligned as analogous because the role in the theory is parallel (the canonical 'JL' statement of each paper) even though the conclusions differ.

Paper B frames the problem (random projection / dimensionality reduction) as a separate Problem node citing Johnson-Lindenstrauss 1984; paper A's main theorem is the corresponding 'extension' face of the same 1984 paper. Both nodes name the JL setup as the underlying problem, hence analogous.

Both lemmas are the central concentration ingredient driving the sqrt(log n) factor. Paper A bounds E[max of m squared standard Gaussians] <~ log m (any dependence). Paper B gives a sharper IID concentration: averages of d squared 1-sub-Gaussians deviate by eps with probability <= 2 exp(-d (eps^2 - eps^3)/4). Same flavor (squared (sub-)Gaussian moments), different formulation (max-of-many vs. average-of-d, dependent vs. iid, expectation vs. tail), so analogous rather than exact.

Paper A's equation EP448.2 is the displayed form of the 'expected max of squared Gaussians is <~ log m' bound, which corresponds in role to paper B's iid concentration proposition for averages of squared sub-Gaussians. Analogous as the displayed-equation counterpart of the lemma already aligned above.

Both invoke the same Gaussian / sub-Gaussian linearity property: a normalized linear combination of iid (sub-)Gaussians is (sub-)Gaussian with the right variance. Paper A states it as a lemma giving an isometric embedding R^n -> L_2(Omega) via Gaussians; paper B uses it as a single proof step verifying that Z_i = sum_j (y_j/||y||) T_ij is 1-sub-Gaussian. Same algebraic fact, different framing.

Both are the proofs of the central concentration ingredient. Paper A proves E[max G_i^2] <~ log m by Gaussian tail + union bound + tail integration with the substitution s = 2 log m. Paper B proves the iid sub-Gaussian deviation via a Chernoff argument using the 'Gaussian trick' MGF identity (right tail) and a fourth-moment Taylor bound (left tail). Conceptually parallel proofs of the analogous concentration lemmas.

Composite L2 alignment between the inner step DAGs of the two concentration proofs (PP448.2 and PP462.1, already matched above). Paper A: tail bound -> union bound -> tail integration -> substitute s = 2 log m. Paper B: Gaussian-trick MGF for upper tail -> Chernoff optimization -> fourth-moment Taylor for lower tail -> Chernoff optimization. Both are 'Chernoff-style' arguments producing a logarithmic concentration constant, but paper B replaces tail-integration with Chernoff/MGF and adds a separate left-tail argument. Aligned as one composite analogous match.

Both are the proofs of the headline JL-type theorem in their respective papers, both built around the same scaffold: introduce a (sub-)Gaussian random projection, show that the squared norms concentrate around the right value, and conclude existence by a probabilistic / max-tail argument over O(n^2) pairs. Paper A: Gaussian isometry + coordinate-wise McShane extension + projection back, with the conclusion driven by a max-of-squared-Gaussians bound. Paper B: scaled iid sub-Gaussian projection + per-pair concentration + union bound. Different scaffolds for different theorems but parallel logical structure.

Composite L2 match between the analogous final concentration + union-bound steps inside the two main proofs. Paper A bounds Lip(U) by sqrt(E max squared Gaussians) over n^2 pairs, then plugs in the log n bound. Paper B applies the squared-sub-Gaussian concentration to each Z_i^2 and unions over the binom(n,2) pairs. Both convert per-pair concentration over ~n^2 events into an existence statement, yielding the log n factor.

Definition of the Lipschitz constant is central to paper A (the entire theorem is about extending Lipschitz maps) but has no counterpart in paper B, which works exclusively with norms and quasi-isometry constants on a fixed finite point set.

The displayed Lipschitz bound on the extension U in terms of E[max squared Gaussian] is paper A's bookkeeping equation tying the extension construction to the concentration ingredient; paper B's analogous role is filled by the per-pair concentration statement EP462.4 / EP462.5, but those are tail bounds rather than the L_2(Omega) Lipschitz inequality, so a direct match would mislead. Marked none.

Remark on an alternative derivation via Ball's extension theorem combined with Markov-type 2 estimates is specific to the extension-theoretic literature and has no counterpart in paper B's sparse-projection treatment.

Historical remark that the original JL 1984 proof used dimension reduction (which paper A explicitly avoids) has no analogue in paper B. Paper B in fact embraces dimension reduction as its central mechanism, so the contrast is informative for the pair-level relation but not an alignable node.
Definition of a q-sparse random matrix is original to paper B (the whole 'sparsity' axis of the title) and absent from paper A, which uses dense Gaussians.
(kappa, kappa', s)-full vector is a paper-B specific structural condition on the input data points, with no counterpart in paper A.

Sparse projection matrix A = zeta * U / sqrt(dq) is the central object of paper B; paper A's projection (k^{-1} P U) lives in a different setting (Hilbert-space coordinates, not a sparse random matrix), so no analogue.

Quasi-isometry equation displayed for paper B's JL-lemma statement; paper A's analogous notion would be the Lipschitz extension condition Lip(F) <~ sqrt(log n) Lip(f), which is captured in TP448.1 itself. No standalone equation counterpart in paper A.

The 'Gaussian trick' identity e^{l x^2} = integral form is a key technical tool in paper B's MGF arguments. Paper A proves the squared-Gaussian bound directly via tail integration without the Gaussian-trick identity, so this equation has no specific counterpart in paper A's proof.
Achlioptas-optimality (P(X=0) <= 2/3 for 1-sub-Gaussian variance-1 X) is original to paper B and centrally about sparsity, with no counterpart in paper A.
Hanson-Wright-style moment bound for non-negative quadratic forms is paper B's main technical proposition for the high-probability sparse JL theorem; paper A uses no quadratic-form concentration.
Sparse JL with target dimension Theta(log n / eps^2) is a paper-B contribution about sparse projection matrices; not present in paper A.
High-probability sparse JL with poly-log target dimension is original to paper B.
Optimality theorem on the sparsity threshold q ~ 1/s is paper B's lower-bound contribution and has no counterpart in paper A.

Right-tail Chernoff bound for averages of squared sub-Gaussians; the analogous role on paper A's side is filled by the integrated bound on E[max G_i^2], already captured in the LP448.1 / PrP462.1 alignment. Listed as none to avoid double-counting.
Left-tail Chernoff bound; paper A's max-of-squared-Gaussians lemma is one-sided in expectation, so there is no separate left-tail counterpart on the paper-A side.

Classical JL dimension condition d >= 8 log n / (eps^2 - eps^3) is the dimension-reduction statement; paper A's analogous quantitative outcome is the sqrt(log n) Lipschitz-blow-up factor in TP448.1, already aligned. No separate displayed equation in paper A.
Proof of Achlioptas-optimality is paper-B specific.
Proof of the Hanson-Wright-style bound is paper-B specific; paper A neither states nor proves a quadratic-form moment bound.
Proof of the sparse JL theorem (Theta(log n / eps^2) version) is original to paper B.
Proof of the high-probability sparse JL theorem is original to paper B.
Proof of the sparsity-optimality (lower-bound) theorem is paper-B specific.
